The rest of this paper is a response to them.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"what-this-paper-is-and-is-not\"\u003EWhat this paper is, and is not\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EIt is a defensive, practical guide for security and IT leaders in mid-size organizations. It uses the modern battlefield as a lens, and every lesson ends in something you can do.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EIt is not a weapons paper. It does not describe how to build, buy, aim or defeat any weapon. It contains no targeting content and no training content. When it speaks of testing, it means authorized, scoped testing of your own systems, performed with written permission. It does not recommend striking back at anyone. Responses to attackers belong to law enforcement and to people with authority and evidence.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EIt is not a vendor list. It makes no promise that any product, or any plan in this paper, will produce a particular result for you.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch1 id=\"the-modern-battlefield\"\u003EThe modern battlefield, read by a security analyst\u003C\/h1\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ELet me be plain about what I am doing here, and what I am not.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EI am reading public analysis of modern conflict for general lessons about technology. I am not assessing any government, army or leader. I make no claim about any party. This paper draws general lessons about technology and conflict from public sources. It takes no side and makes no claim about any party.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EI leave out casualty, loss and performance figures for every side. They are contested. They are estimates. And they are not what a security team needs to make a decision. I also leave out the attribution that some sources attach to specific events. That is not because it does not matter. It is because I am not the right author to judge it, and the lesson does not depend on it.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EWhat I keep are the phenomena. Drone saturation. Jamming and spoofing. Sensor transparency. Cheap mass. Logistics under observation. Decentralized decisions.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"the-framing\"\u003EThe framing\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EMy shorthand: trench-style grind fused with science fiction.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThink of the first world war’s long stalemate, the lines of dug-in positions where nothing moved fast. Now add cheap drones overhead, signals jammed and spoofed, satellites and commercial sensors watching the ground, and a cycle of measure and countermeasure that turns over in weeks.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECSIS opens its chapter on technological evolution with the point that new technology drives tactics in unprecedented ways, and that “the party that innovates, procures, and adapts first secures an often insurmountable edge.” It gives an example from the first world war: the development of the first rudimentary tank to break the stalemate of trench warfare (CSIS, 2025a).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EIt then offers the line I keep coming back to: “the next generation of warfare will not be defined solely by who possesses the most advanced technology, but by who can integrate, adapt, and counter it the fastest” (CSIS, 2025a).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EIntegrate. Adapt. Counter. That is a good description of a security program.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"what-public-analysis-describes\"\u003EWhat public analysis describes\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EHere are the features I draw on, with the source for each.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ECheap, flexible sensing and strike.\u003C\/strong\u003E CSIS says the most marked change has been cheap, flexible and highly maneuverable intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) drones. It says cover and concealment are “of the utmost importance,” and that large, highly visible formations are more vulnerable to drone strikes (CSIS, 2025a).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EA cat-and-mouse cycle.\u003C\/strong\u003E CSIS describes “a highly iterative game of cat and mouse, with advancements in electronic warfare meeting drone advancements step for step” (CSIS, 2025a). It quotes an analyst describing a “six week learning cycle on the battlefield” (CSIS, 2025a).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EElectronic warfare as the norm.\u003C\/strong\u003E In its chapter on space, CSIS calls the pervasiveness of electronic warfare (EW) “one of the most dominant features of the modern battlefield.” It describes EW as a “temporary and reversible way” to target satellite navigation, communications signals and ISR collection, and says “going forward, EW will be the norm” (CSIS, 2025b). It also warns that regions outside conflict zones will experience greater electromagnetic interference, risking harm to civil and commercial transportation and public safety (CSIS, 2025b).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ETransparency.\u003C\/strong\u003E CSIS says commercial space capabilities have introduced “a new level of transparency” and that “all militaries must adapt to a world where movements, emissions, and signatures are constantly monitored” (CSIS, 2025b). A separate CSIS chapter on intelligence says wars of the future will be fought “in conditions of near transparency,” and that “information is cheap. Processing it is expensive, and sense-making is exquisite” (CSIS, 2025c).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ELogistics under pressure.\u003C\/strong\u003E CSIS says logistics chains “will be in constant peril” and that modern armies “need to anticipate that only a fraction of supplies will get through” (CSIS, 2025a).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EDecentralized units.\u003C\/strong\u003E CSIS says the future is shifting toward “smaller, highly mobile, adaptable units, where field commanders are empowered to make decisions” while minimizing their communications signature (CSIS, 2025a).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ENo clean front line.\u003C\/strong\u003E CSIS warns that as commercial providers take on greater roles in military operations, the line between combatants and noncombatants will blur, and that civilian service providers such as those supplying power, cloud storage and internet connectivity could increasingly be seen as military targets (CSIS, 2025a). That is CSIS’s forecast, and it is contested ground in law and policy. I cite it as a warning about dependency, not as a statement of law.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EOverdependence.\u003C\/strong\u003E CSIS says militaries “will need to incorporate technology without depending on it,” and that “a force multiplier is a high-priority target for an opponent” (CSIS, 2025a).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"five-fronts\"\u003EFive fronts\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EI organize the lessons into five fronts, and add two more that cut across all of them: command and people.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ctable\u003E\n\u003Cthead\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003EFront\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003EWhat public analysis describes\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003EThe same feature on your network\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003C\/thead\u003E\n\u003Ctbody\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ETrenches\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EDefenders who can dig in with effective counter-drone measures hold an advantage; cover and concealment matter\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EDepth: segmentation, identity at every line, a small trust zone\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EDrones\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ECheap, numerous, flexible; economics favor the cheap\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EAutomated scanning, credential stuffing, floods, bots; cheap automated controls in reply\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EElectronic warfare\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EJamming and spoofing of signals; EW is the norm\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ESpoofed identities, time, names and voices; verify out of band; keep a second source\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ESensors\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ENear-transparency; assume you are seen\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EExposed surface; edge devices; your own telemetry; deception\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ESupply lines\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ELogistics in constant peril; commercial dependencies\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ESuppliers, cloud, platforms; offline copies; manual fallbacks\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ECommand\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EDecentralized units; fast learning cycles\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EDecision rights; out-of-band comms; short lessons-learned loops\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EPeople\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EEndurance, integrated technology without overdependence\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EStaffing, rotation, skill; AI as a helper, not a crutch\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003C\/tbody\u003E\n\u003C\/table\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"where-the-comparison-breaks\"\u003EWhere the comparison breaks\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EI owe you the limits.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EA network is not terrain. You cannot dig a trench in an IP range. And you can restore a server from a backup, which is not something a lost position allows.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EYour adversaries are not armies. Most of the pressure on a mid-size organization comes from criminals, opportunists and automated tools. Some comes from more capable actors. The lens helps with the shape of the contest. It does not tell you who is on the other end.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EStatistics do not transfer. A figure from a battlefield study tells you nothing about your firewall. That is why I use no battlefield statistics at all. My numbers come from breach and incident research, and I cite them to their sources.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EDo not mistake analogy for instruction. This paper does not tell you to take any action against any adversary. Offensive action by private organizations raises legal and safety problems, and it is not what this paper recommends.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EFinally, a caution about the analogy itself. The point of the lens is not drama. The point is that long, cheap, constant pressure is a different problem from a single dramatic attack, and it needs a different kind of plan.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ENow the fronts, one at a time.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch1 id=\"analysis\"\u003EAnalysis: five fronts and two cross-cutting concerns\u003C\/h1\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThe next seven parts take the fronts in turn. Each part follows the same pattern: what public sources describe, what it means for your network, what to do, and what to measure.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"part-i-trenches\"\u003EPart I: Trenches. Depth beats a hard shell\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWhat public analysis describes.\u003C\/strong\u003E CSIS says that “defenders who can dig in with effective counter-drone measures will have a significant advantage, and those who must cross open land will be at a significant disadvantage” (CSIS, 2025a). It adds that cover and concealment are of the utmost importance (CSIS, 2025a).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ETwo ideas there. Depth. And making the attacker cross open ground.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWhat it means for you.\u003C\/strong\u003E For thirty years, many networks were built like a shell. Hard outside. Soft inside. One firewall and a VPN. Get past the wall and you can walk anywhere.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ENIST’s zero trust guidance describes the problem with a picture from an airport. All passengers pass a security checkpoint, then mill about the terminal, “and all the individuals are considered trusted.” That boarding area is what NIST calls the “implicit trust zone.” NIST then makes the point that matters: “the implicit trust zone must be as small as possible” for the policy decision point to be as specific as it can be (NIST SP 800-207, 2020).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EShrink the zone where everyone is trusted. That is the whole idea.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ENIST defines zero trust as “an evolving set of cybersecurity paradigms that move defenses from static, network-based perimeters to focus on users, assets, and resources.” It assumes “no implicit trust granted to assets or user accounts based solely on their physical or network location” (NIST SP 800-207, 2020).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EIts tenets read like a field order for a defender who expects to be penetrated:\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EAll communication is secured regardless of network location. Network location alone does not imply trust.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EAccess to individual resources is granted on a per-session basis, with the least privileges needed.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EAccess is determined by dynamic policy, including client identity, application and the requesting asset, and may include behavioral and environmental attributes.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EThe enterprise monitors and measures the integrity and security posture of all owned and associated assets. No asset is inherently trusted.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EAuthentication and authorization are dynamic and strictly enforced before access is allowed.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EThe enterprise collects as much information as possible about the current state of assets, network infrastructure and communications, and uses it to improve its security posture (NIST SP 800-207, 2020).\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ENIST is honest about the limits: these tenets are “the ideal goal,” and not all may be fully implemented in their purest form (NIST SP 800-207, 2020).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"why-depth-matters-in-a-war-of-attrition\"\u003EWhy depth matters in a war of attrition\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EAn attacker with persistence will eventually get a foothold. A phished account. An exposed edge device. A stolen credential. Verizon notes that attackers are “increasingly blending in with normal operations by using the same access paths as legitimate users,” such as desktop-sharing tools and virtual private networks (Verizon, 2026). It adds that threat actors seem to be dialing back reliance on traditional tools such as Cobalt Strike as defenders get better at detecting and blocking them (Verizon, 2026).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThat is measure and countermeasure in your own logs. The contest moved. Your design has to assume the first line will be crossed.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ENIST’s cyber resiliency guidance names the design moves. Among its techniques:\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ECoordinated protection.\u003C\/strong\u003E “Require a threat event to overcome multiple safeguards,” increasing the cost to the adversary and the likelihood of detection.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ESegmentation.\u003C\/strong\u003E Contain adversary activity to the enclave, segment or facility where it has established a presence, limiting where malware can propagate.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ERealignment.\u003C\/strong\u003E Minimize connections between mission-critical and non-critical services, so that a failure in the latter does not reach the former.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EPrivilege restriction.\u003C\/strong\u003E Make the adversary invest more time and effort obtaining credentials, and curtail what stolen credentials can do.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EDiversity.\u003C\/strong\u003E Use heterogeneity to minimize common-mode failures and make the adversary build tools for more than one target type (NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 2 Rev. 1, 2021).\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThe same document is candid about costs. It notes that “diversity and segmentation can each make analytic monitoring and contextual awareness more difficult,” because diverse systems need tools that can handle the variety, and segmentation can limit visibility (NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 2 Rev. 1, 2021).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EDepth is not free. Each line you dig has to be manned, watched and maintained. A trench line nobody patrols is a ditch.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"the-trench-map\"\u003EThe trench map\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EHere is a simple way to lay it out. I call these lines. They are my own organizing device, drawn from the NIST and CISA material above. They are not a standard.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ctable\u003E\n\u003Cthead\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003ELine\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003EQuestion it answers\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003ETypical controls\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003EWhat to watch\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003C\/thead\u003E\n\u003Ctbody\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003E0. The edge\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EWhat does the internet touch?\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EInventory of internet-facing assets; patching of edge devices; removal of unused services; management interfaces off the internet\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EExposure count; time to patch known-exploited flaws\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003E1. Identity\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EWho or what is asking?\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EPhishing-resistant multifactor authentication; per-session access; least privilege; service-account inventory\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EPrivileged accounts; dormant accounts; unusual sign-ins\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003E2. Segments\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EHow far can one foothold travel?\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ENetwork and application segmentation; separate management network; restricted east-west traffic\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ECross-segment flows; new connections between systems that never talk\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003E3. Crown assets\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EWhat cannot be lost?\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EData classification; stronger controls and logging around critical systems; separate admin paths\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EAccess to crown data; unusual bulk reads\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003E4. Recovery\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EHow do we come back?\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ETested, isolated backups; rebuild runbooks; alternate communications\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ERestore time actually achieved in rehearsal\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003C\/tbody\u003E\n\u003C\/table\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EFour of those five lines do not stop the attacker. They slow, contain, expose and survive. That is the point. In attrition, nothing is impenetrable. The goal is to make every step cost more than it is worth, and to see it happening.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"a-maturity-ladder-you-can-borrow\"\u003EA maturity ladder you can borrow\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECISA’s Zero Trust Maturity Model is written for federal agencies, but its structure helps anyone. It organizes zero trust into five pillars: Identity, Devices, Networks, Applications and Workloads, and Data. It adds three cross-cutting capabilities: Visibility and Analytics, Automation and Orchestration, and Governance. It describes maturity in four stages: Traditional, Initial, Advanced and Optimal. Each pillar can progress at its own pace (CISA ZTMM, 2023).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EIn the Networks pillar, the model’s progression runs from large perimeter or macro-segmentation, through isolation of critical workloads and expanded ingress and egress micro-perimeters, toward micro-segmentation around application profiles (CISA ZTMM, 2023).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EFor a mid-size organization, treat “Optimal” as a direction, not a deadline. Move each pillar one stage at a time. The stage you are in matters less than whether you know it, and whether you can show movement from quarter to quarter.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"what-to-do_1\"\u003EWhat to do\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Col\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EDraw your real lines.\u003C\/strong\u003E Take the five lines above and write, for each, what you have today. Be blunt. Mark each as strong, partial or absent.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EShrink the implicit trust zone.\u003C\/strong\u003E Start with the most valuable segment. Move administrative access onto a separate path. Require phishing-resistant authentication for administrators and remote access first.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ESegment before you buy.\u003C\/strong\u003E Segmentation that exists on a diagram does not count. Test it. Try to reach a crown system from an ordinary workstation, with permission, and write down what happens.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EPay the monitoring cost.\u003C\/strong\u003E For every line you add, decide what telemetry crosses it and who looks at it.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EKeep it boring.\u003C\/strong\u003E Simple designs that people understand survive staff turnover. Elaborate ones decay.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ol\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"what-to-measure\"\u003EWhat to measure\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ENumber of segments that contain crown assets, and number of rules allowing traffic into them.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EShare of administrator and remote-access accounts using phishing-resistant authentication.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ENumber of systems in the implicit trust zone: those a single compromised workstation can reach.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ETime to restore a crown system from backup, in a rehearsal.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EDo not compare your numbers with a survey median. Compare them with your own last quarter.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"part-ii-drones\"\u003EPart II: Drones. Cheap mass against your attention\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWhat public analysis describes.\u003C\/strong\u003E The economics come first. CSIS puts them in one line: “If a $500 drone can destroy a multimillion-dollar tank, so, too, can a USV swarm destroy a fleet of ships” (CSIS, 2025a). That is a statement about cost asymmetry, not a measurement of how often it happens. CSIS also says “counter-drone solutions will be decisive on the future battlefield” (CSIS, 2025a), and describes the most marked change as cheap, flexible and highly maneuverable ISR drones (CSIS, 2025a).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECheap. Many. Flexible. The answer to it is not one exquisite shield. It is a layered, cheap, repeatable defense, and a way to keep from running out of it.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWhat it means for you.\u003C\/strong\u003E Your drones are not aircraft. They are software. Automated scanning for exposed services. Credential stuffing against login pages. Bot traffic. Floods. Commodity phishing kits sold as a service. ENISA describes Phishing-as-a-Service as “automation that paves the way for attackers regardless of their experience” (ENISA, 2025). The same logic as the drone: low cost, low skill, high volume.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThe 2026 Verizon DBIR gives a sense of the scale on the flooding side. Its year-in-review timeline records a botnet of 300,000 internet-of-things hosts launching a record 29.7 Tbps DDoS attack, nearly doubling previous peaks (Verizon, 2026). Meanwhile, the median attack size has stayed between 4.2 and 6 Gbps, and half of all attacks last under nine minutes (Verizon, 2026). Both things are true. The peaks grow. The routine stays small and cheap.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EFor an organization your size, the peak is a vendor problem. The routine is yours.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"the-cost-exchange\"\u003EThe cost exchange\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EHere is the exchange in plain terms. The left column is the attacker’s cheap move. The right column is the defender’s cheap answer. This is my summary, built on the sources cited in this part. It is not a measured result.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ctable\u003E\n\u003Cthead\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003ECheap move against you\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003EWhat it costs you if unanswered\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003ECheap answer\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003C\/thead\u003E\n\u003Ctbody\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EAutomated login attempts using stolen credentials\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EAccount takeover; investigation time\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EMultifactor authentication on externally exposed applications and remote access; lockout and rate limits\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EMass phishing and pretexting\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EAnalyst time per report; a successful click\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EPhishing-resistant authentication; reporting button; verification rules for payment and identity requests\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EScans for old, exposed services\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EOne unpatched edge device is a way in\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EInventory of the edge; automated patching; remove what you do not use\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EShort flood bursts, repeated\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EOutage minutes; staff pulled off other work\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EUpstream DDoS protection; a rehearsed runbook; clear thresholds for escalation\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EAI bot traffic hitting sites and APIs\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EBandwidth, content exposure, noise\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ERate limits; bot management; robots rules; monitoring\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003C\/tbody\u003E\n\u003C\/table\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ENotice what is in the right column. No miracle. Authentication, patching, inventory, capacity and a plan.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EVerizon’s mitigation guidance for exploited vulnerabilities and stolen credentials lines up with the table: require MFA for externally exposed applications and for remote network access, and perform automated operating system and application patch management (Verizon, 2026).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"plan-for-the-tail-not-the-average\"\u003EPlan for the tail, not the average\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EVerizon gives numbers worth building a runbook around. For the repeatedly attacked DDoS victims in its sample, Verizon reports a median attack duration of 24 minutes. At the higher end of the distribution, it puts duration at around 88 minutes at the 90th percentile and 101 minutes at the 95th (Verizon, 2026).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ESo design for roughly two hours. Ask three questions.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Col\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EWhich customer-facing or revenue-critical services would be unavailable for two hours, and what would that cost?\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EWho decides when to switch to the upstream mitigation or the backup path, and what do they need to know?\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EWhat does the rest of the team do during a flood? Verizon’s own question is the right one: “What would be the impact to your business if your business was affected?” (Verizon, 2026).\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ol\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EOne caution, and it is my judgment, not a finding. Treat any flood as a possible distraction. While your eyes are on the loud problem, check the quiet ones. Make sure someone is assigned to do exactly that.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"counter-drone-for-the-network-four-layers\"\u003ECounter-drone for the network: four layers\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EAbsorb.\u003C\/strong\u003E Put capacity between the flood and your service. For most mid-size organizations, that means buying protection from an upstream provider rather than building it. Ask for written answers on how it works, how fast it engages, and what it costs when attacks run long.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EFilter.\u003C\/strong\u003E Rate limits, bot management, geo and reputation rules where they make sense, and strong authentication on every login surface. Verizon notes that defenders have to “maintain our footing and use collaboration and partnerships” against growing attacker capability (Verizon, 2026). Sharing with peers and providers counts as a layer.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EAutomate.\u003C\/strong\u003E Cheap and repeatable. Patch automation. Configuration baselines. Alert enrichment. IBM found that security teams extensively using AI and automation shortened breach times by 65 days and lowered average costs by USD 1.93 million compared with those that did not. Only 36% of breached organizations said they used these tools extensively across the security lifecycle (IBM and Ponemon Institute, 2026). That is an association in a benchmark study. It is not proof of what a tool will do for you. But the direction is clear: volume answered by automation.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EIntercept, with a human on the trigger.\u003C\/strong\u003E Automated response can contain a compromised account or isolate a host faster than a person can. It can also cause an outage faster than any attacker. Start every automated action in recommend-only mode. Widen authority as evidence supports it. Keep a clear off switch and a named owner.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECSIS gives the right caution from the battlefield side: when both sides have AI-enabled systems, “the incentive will lean heavily toward deferring as much as possible to the AI’s capability,” and “for now, that surely will lead to mistakes” (CSIS, 2025a). Replace “targeting” with “triage” and the warning still holds. Do not let your people turn into a stamp of approval.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"the-next-turn-of-the-cycle\"\u003EThe next turn of the cycle\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECSIS offers a forecast, flagged as a forecast. It says sophisticated adversaries will probably find ways to combine AI and cyberattacks, with “offense likely outstripping defense at first,” and that AI agents will be able to find vulnerabilities and exploit them “without phoning home and raising alarms” (CSIS, 2025a). Treat that as a planning assumption, not as a fact.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EWhat follows from it? Shorter patch windows on the edge. More weight on detection of behavior over indicators. More automation on your side, built on the same cheap controls.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"what-to-do_2\"\u003EWhat to do\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Col\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWrite the cost-exchange table for your own organization.\u003C\/strong\u003E Five rows. Their move, your cost, your cheap answer. Fill in the missing right-hand cells and fund the gaps.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EPut MFA on every externally exposed login and every remote access path.\u003C\/strong\u003E Administrators and remote access first.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EAutomate patching on the edge.\u003C\/strong\u003E Set a target time for known-exploited vulnerabilities on internet-facing systems, and track it.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EBuy absorption, do not build it.\u003C\/strong\u003E Get upstream flood protection in writing, and run a rehearsal.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ERun the two-hour drill.\u003C\/strong\u003E Simulate a two-hour outage of one customer-facing service and note what breaks.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EStart automation in recommend-only mode,\u003C\/strong\u003E and review overrides weekly.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ol\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"what-to-measure_1\"\u003EWhat to measure\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EMedian time to remediate known-exploited vulnerabilities on internet-facing systems (your baseline, not a survey median).\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EShare of external login surfaces protected by multifactor authentication.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EMean time from flood detection to mitigation engagement, in rehearsal.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EAnalyst hours spent per week on repetitive triage, and the share handled by automation with human review.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"part-iii-electronic-warfare\"\u003EPart III: Electronic warfare. When the signal lies\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWhat public analysis describes.\u003C\/strong\u003E Jamming blocks a signal. Spoofing sends a false one. A note from three EU member states to the Council of the EU defines them plainly: jamming is deliberate radio interference “when information about an aircraft location, altitude, and time is not received,” and spoofing is deliberate interference in which wrong signals are sent “and aircraft location, altitude, and time are displayed incorrectly” (Council of the EU, 2025).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECSIS calls the pervasiveness of EW one of the most dominant features of the modern battlefield, and a “temporary and reversible way” to degrade satellite navigation and communications. It says EW will be the norm, and that militaries will place “a premium on operating effectively in degraded environments” (CSIS, 2025b).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThe effects reach civilians. IATA data, cited in a joint release with the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), says GPS signal loss events increased 220% between 2021 and 2024 (EASA and IATA, 2025). EASA’s Flight Standards Director put the strategic shift this way: “We are no longer just containing GNSS interference — we must build resilience” (EASA and IATA, 2025). The Finnish Transport and Communications Agency reported that disruptions in the Gulf of Finland had “already caused near misses,” that signal disruptions “may cause unexpected malfunctions, for example in vessels’ autopilot functions,” and that spoofing of the Automatic Identification System, where incorrect data is fed in, “has also become more frequent” (Traficom, 2025).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EAnd note what it says next: “alongside AIS, other systems are also used to verify data on the location and movement of ships” (Traficom, 2025). A second source.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWhat it means for you.\u003C\/strong\u003E This is the part of the battlefield that travels furthest into your network. Not the jammer. The principle. When the thing a machine trusts can be falsified, every decision built on it is exposed.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThe Council note adds the point that matters for your clocks. Satellite navigation systems provide positioning, navigation and timing. The timing services “also serve for time synchronization of telecommunication networks, and, thus, are vital to enable seamless communication, synchronize financial transactions, stabilize power grids, etc.” (Council of the EU, 2025).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"your-time-is-a-signal\"\u003EYour time is a signal\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EMost security teams do not think about time as a dependency. They should.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ENIST’s Foundational Positioning, Navigation and Timing (PNT) profile tells organizations to identify all software, applications and systems that depend on PNT data, including those that rely on distributed time. Its examples of dependent applications include “test and measurement tools, kernels, databases, logging software, cryptography\/certificate management, and other software that rely on synchronized clocks or positioning information” (NIST IR 8323r1, 2023).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ERead that again with your own stack in mind. Logging. Certificates. Databases. If your time source is wrong, your logs are out of order, your certificates may fail validation, and your incident timeline is fiction.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThe profile’s advice on testing is concrete. For systems with redundant or complementary time sources, validate by “removing the primary time source and confirming that the time accuracy and precision” meet pre-defined requirements for the time server and downstream applications (NIST IR 8323r1, 2023). It also says to prioritize “maintaining essential functions despite system disruption or manipulation” (NIST IR 8323r1, 2023).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ETest it. Pull the primary time source in a controlled window, with change approval, and see what breaks.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"other-signals-that-can-lie\"\u003EOther signals that can lie\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ETime is the least visible. The rest are more familiar.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EIdentity.\u003C\/strong\u003E A login that is valid, from a device that looks right, by someone who is not who they say. Verizon found credential abuse is pervasive: considering all instances of credential abuse at any point in a breach, it sits at 39% (Verizon, 2026).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EVoice and text.\u003C\/strong\u003E Verizon draws a line between phishing, which it describes as an essentially asynchronous social action, and pretexting, which “intrinsically involves a synchronous component”: someone on the other end of a call or thread, trying to convince a person to do something they should not. It warns that the countermeasures and training for the two are distinct (Verizon, 2026). Help-desk impersonation is a live example. IBM reports that social engineering such as impersonating help desk staff was used in 13% of attacks and led to average breach costs of USD 5.23 million, and that voice and SMS phishing, used in 17% of attacks, led to the highest average costs among attack vectors at USD 5.29 million (IBM and Ponemon Institute, 2026).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ESynthetic media.\u003C\/strong\u003E CSIS says adversaries are already employing AI for deepfakes meant to sow doubt and confusion, and forecasts that the next iteration “could entail deepfake military orders” and realistic denial and deception operations designed to sow tactical chaos (CSIS, 2025a). It adds that, with adversarial AI generating deception at machine speeds, “trust in such information will be tested” (CSIS, 2025b). Your version is a deepfaked executive voice asking finance for an urgent transfer. That is a scenario, not a statistic. The controls are not exotic.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"the-second-source\"\u003EThe second source\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EDead reckoning, the theme of the first paper in this series, is the habit of navigating without a signal: last known position, heading, speed, time and a second source. Here is the network version.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ctable\u003E\n\u003Cthead\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003ESignal you trust\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003EWhat can go wrong\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003ESecond source\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003EDrill\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003C\/thead\u003E\n\u003Ctbody\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ETime\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EDrift or false time from a single source\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EAt least two independent time sources; alert on divergence\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ERemove the primary source in a change window and check logs, certificates and authentication\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EIdentity\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EStolen or replayed credentials; impersonated help-desk requests\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EDevice posture; a second factor that resists phishing; call-back to a known number for sensitive requests\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ETest the help-desk verification procedure with an authorized, scoped exercise\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EVoice and video\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ESynthetic or impersonated speakers\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EOut-of-band verification through a known channel; pre-agreed words for urgent requests\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ERun a payment-approval drill in which the “boss” is not real\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EName and routing data\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EAltered answers from systems you rely on\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ECross-check against an independent resolver or source; log and alert on changes\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ECompare answers from two sources on critical names during a review\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EAlerts and logs\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EA tool that goes silent, or a log source that stops\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EHeartbeat checks; a second detection path for crown assets\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ESilence one sensor and see how long it takes anyone to notice\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003C\/tbody\u003E\n\u003C\/table\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EI will not describe how to carry out any of these attacks. The point of the table is the right-hand columns.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"degraded-operations\"\u003EDegraded operations\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECSIS says the future will require using technology “without depending on it.” It gives the example of a force that depends entirely on satellite navigation, which could find itself “toothless” if the signal goes dark, and notes that one academy is teaching navigation by the stars as a coping mechanism. It says that if a drone swarm is taken down by electronic warfare, the unit “must be able to fight on” (CSIS, 2025a).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EYour version: what do we do when the tool is down? Not the SIEM is slow. The SIEM is gone. Not the VPN is flaky. The VPN is the problem.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECSIS also describes a technical adaptation: fiber-optic tethers, which it calls “impervious to jamming” (CSIS, 2025a) and which “eliminate reliance on wireless signals” (CSIS, 2025b). The defender’s analog is simple. Keep a wired, separate, out-of-band path to manage your most important systems. If the path you use to fix the network is the network you are fixing, you have one point of failure.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"what-to-do_3\"\u003EWhat to do\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Col\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EList your signals.\u003C\/strong\u003E Time, identity, names, voice, alerts. For each, name the second source.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ERun two independent time sources,\u003C\/strong\u003E and alert when they disagree. Then test removing the primary one.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ESet verification rules\u003C\/strong\u003E for payment, credential reset and access requests. Use a callback to a number you already hold. Make the rule easy to follow and impossible to skip, even for the most senior person.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ERehearse degraded operations.\u003C\/strong\u003E Once a quarter, run one critical process with a tool unavailable. Use the old checklist. Write down what was missing.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EBuild an out-of-band management path\u003C\/strong\u003E for your most critical systems and keep it separate from daily use.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ETreat synthetic media as a normal risk.\u003C\/strong\u003E Train the people who move money and reset accounts, and give them the authority to say no.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ol\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"what-to-measure_2\"\u003EWhat to measure\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ENumber of independent time sources per critical system, and time to detect drift between them.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EShare of sensitive requests verified through an out-of-band channel.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ETime for the team to notice a silenced log source in a drill.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ETime to complete a critical business process in degraded mode, against normal mode.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"part-iv-sensors\"\u003EPart IV: Sensors. Assume you are being watched\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWhat public analysis describes.\u003C\/strong\u003E CSIS says commercial sensors have changed the battlefield. “All militaries must adapt to a world where movements, emissions, and signatures are constantly monitored.” It adds that forces, “especially those at fixed sites and massed in central locations, must assume that they will be seen and their movements and emissions detected.” Its prescription is “renewed emphasis on operational security, deception tactics, and electromagnetic spectrum discipline,” with exercises that “simulate conditions where adversaries possess near-real-time ISR capabilities” (CSIS, 2025b).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EA second CSIS chapter makes the human point. “Information is cheap. Processing it is expensive, and sense-making is exquisite.” It also warns that rival services can use video data and a person’s “digital dust” to reveal an identity that was meant to stay hidden (CSIS, 2025c).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ETwo lessons. Your signature is visible. And your own sensors only help if you can make sense of what they tell you.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWhat it means for you.\u003C\/strong\u003E Start from the adversary’s side of the glass. MITRE’s ATT\u0026amp;CK framework opens its list of tactics with Reconnaissance: “The adversary is trying to gather information they can use to plan future operations.” The tactic covers adversaries “actively or passively gathering information that can be used to support targeting,” and the information “may include details of the victim organization, infrastructure, or staff\/personnel” (MITRE ATT\u0026amp;CK, TA0043). Its technique list includes active scanning of IP blocks and vulnerabilities, gathering host, identity and network information, and searching open websites and technical databases.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EYou are scanned all day. Most of it is noise. Some of it is a survey.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"your-signature\"\u003EYour signature\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EYour signature is everything an outsider can learn about you without breaking in. Think in five layers.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ctable\u003E\n\u003Cthead\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003ELayer\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003EWhat an outsider can see\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003EThe question to ask\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003C\/thead\u003E\n\u003Ctbody\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ENetwork\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EAddress ranges, open services, certificate names, old test systems\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EDoes every internet-facing service have an owner and a reason?\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ESoftware\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EProduct names and versions in banners, headers and file paths\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EDoes the outside need to know which product and version we run?\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EPeople\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ENames, roles, email formats, job postings, public social media\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EWhat does our public staff information say about who holds the keys?\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ECode and cloud\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EPublic repositories, storage buckets, files left shared\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EWhat did we publish by accident, and who checks?\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EBehavior\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EWorking hours, response times, vendor relationships\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EWhat does our rhythm tell a patient observer?\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003C\/tbody\u003E\n\u003C\/table\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThis is not about hiding. Visibility is how business gets done. The goal is to know your signature and make deliberate choices about it, the way a unit chooses where to be seen.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECSIS frames this for militaries as emissions and signature discipline (CSIS, 2025b). Your civilian equivalent is attack surface management. Inventory what is exposed. Remove what is not needed. Patch what must stay. Then look at it again next month, because it will have changed.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"count-what-you-can-see-then-cut\"\u003ECount what you can see, then cut\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThe most valuable signature exercise costs almost nothing. Ask your team to produce a list of everything on the internet that is yours, using the same public sources an outsider would. Compare it with your asset register. The gap between the two lists is the work.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EJoint guidance on network edge devices, released by CISA, NSA and partner agencies in February 2025, points the same way. NSA lists seven mitigation strategies, starting with “know the edge,” and including disabling unneeded features and ports and securing management interfaces (NSA, 2025; CISA, 2025). An NSA expert explains why the edge matters: “if left unsecured, even unskilled malicious cyber actors have an easier time finding and exploiting vulnerabilities in their software or configurations” (NSA, 2025).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"deception-with-limits\"\u003EDeception, with limits\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ENIST’s cyber resiliency guidance includes a Deception technique: “Mislead, confuse, hide critical assets from, or expose covertly tainted assets to the adversary.” It says deception can lead the adversary to waste effort and reveal tactics, techniques and procedures. It also says deception can complicate analytic monitoring and contextual awareness, and that these techniques “come at a cost to some other cyber resiliency objectives” (NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 2 Rev. 1, 2021).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ERemember that when a vendor sells you a deception product. The idea has a long record in adversarial fields. NIST itself notes that Deception, Dynamic Positioning and Unpredictability are cyber adaptations of concepts from adversarial disciplines such as medicine, military and sports (NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 2 Rev. 1, 2021). Used well, a few decoy credentials, files or services that no legitimate user would ever touch give you a near-zero-noise alarm. Used badly, they are one more system to maintain and one more source of confusion.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EMy advice is modest. Start with a small number of decoys in places that matter. Make sure each one raises an alert that a human will see. Do not build a maze you cannot monitor.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"your-own-sensors-the-problem-of-sense-making\"\u003EYour own sensors: the problem of sense-making\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ENow the other direction. What do you see?\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EIBM’s 2026 study found that the mean time to identify and contain a breach was 247 days (IBM and Ponemon Institute, 2026). That is a sense-making number. The evidence was there. Someone had to find it, read it and decide.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECSIS’s line applies exactly: information is cheap, processing it is expensive (CSIS, 2025c). Most mid-size organizations are not short of logs. They are short of attention. Three failure patterns recur:\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Col\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EEverything collected, nothing asked.\u003C\/strong\u003E Terabytes of logs with no question attached.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EAlerts without owners.\u003C\/strong\u003E Detections that fire into a queue nobody is accountable for.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ESensors without a heartbeat.\u003C\/strong\u003E A source that quietly stops, and nobody knows.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ol\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ENIST’s incident response guidance (SP 800-61r3) is now written to sit inside the CSF 2.0 functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover (NIST SP 800-61r3, 2025; NIST CSF 2.0, 2024). That helps. It puts detection beside governance and recovery in one loop, not in a silo.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"a-small-sensor-philosophy\"\u003EA small-sensor philosophy\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EBuild detection from decisions, not from data.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EStart with the five or six decisions you must make fast in an incident. Isolate a host. Disable an account. Take a service offline. Notify a customer or regulator. Call counsel and law enforcement.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EFor each decision, name the signals you need to make it with confidence.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ECollect and retain those signals first. Add more only when a question demands it.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EFor each signal, assign an owner, a response time and a heartbeat check.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EFewer sensors, better understood, beat a sprawl nobody can read.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"keep-your-own-secrets-from-the-wire\"\u003EKeep your own secrets from the wire\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECSIS’s phrase “digital dust” belongs on a poster in your office. Staff leave trails. Contractors leave trails. Old test systems leave trails. Cloud sharing links live forever unless someone ends them. A few steps pay off quickly:\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EReview public repositories, shared drives and storage for exposed secrets and files.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ESet expiry on sharing links and temporary access.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ERotate any credential that has ever appeared in a ticket, chat or document.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EGive staff clear guidance on what not to post about internal systems.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"what-to-do_4\"\u003EWhat to do\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Col\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EMake the outside-in list.\u003C\/strong\u003E Everything public that belongs to you. Reconcile with your asset register. Fix the gaps.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EPick your signature rules.\u003C\/strong\u003E Decide what must be public, what can be reduced, and who approves exceptions.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EDefine your six decisions\u003C\/strong\u003E and the signals behind each one. Retire collection that serves no decision.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EGive every alert an owner and a clock.\u003C\/strong\u003E\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EAdd heartbeats\u003C\/strong\u003E to every critical log source, and test that silence raises an alert.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EStart small on decoys,\u003C\/strong\u003E with legal and privacy sign-off, and only where a human will see the alarm.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EExercise with a watcher in mind.\u003C\/strong\u003E Run one tabletop a year that assumes the adversary has seen your public footprint for months.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ol\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"what-to-measure_3\"\u003EWhat to measure\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ENumber of internet-facing assets without a named owner.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EGap between the outside-in list and your asset register.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EMedian time from alert to first human action.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EShare of critical log sources with a working heartbeat check.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EShare of alerts that lead to a decision, versus alerts closed as noise.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"part-v-supply-lines\"\u003EPart V: Supply lines. The rear is part of the front\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWhat public analysis describes.\u003C\/strong\u003E CSIS says supplying front lines “will be more challenging—and likely deadlier—than ever,” and that modern forces “need to anticipate that only a fraction of supplies will get through.” Forces will therefore “seek to minimize deliveries to the front lines” and adopt technologies that increase self-sufficiency, such as on-site production of parts (CSIS, 2025a). It also says that as commercial providers take on more of the work, the line between combatants and noncombatants blurs: providers of power, cloud storage and internet connectivity could increasingly be seen as legitimate targets (CSIS, 2025a). Read that as a statement about shared infrastructure. In your world, the shared infrastructure is the cloud and the carrier.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EKeep your own parallels in view, and keep them modest. Supply lines are long. They run through other people. They are watched, and they break.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWhat it means for you.\u003C\/strong\u003E Your supply lines are your vendors, your software dependencies, your cloud providers, your connectivity, your managed service providers, your payment processors and your power. Most of it lives outside your walls. You rely on it. You cannot patch it.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"the-numbers-on-dependence\"\u003EThe numbers on dependence\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EVerizon’s 2026 DBIR reports that breaches with third-party involvement increased by 60% from the prior year’s dataset, reaching 48% of total breaches (Verizon, 2026). It describes root causes in many cloud-based third-party incidents that “boil down to insecure authentication (absence of MFA, improper credential rotation) or lack of least privilege enforcement for users or service accounts” (Verizon, 2026). In a survival analysis of third-party cloud exposures, only 23% of organizations had fully remediated missing or improperly secured multifactor authentication, though half of findings were resolved within a month (Verizon, 2026).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EIBM’s 2026 report ranks supply chain compromise as the second most common initial attack vector, and the second slowest to resolve, taking 258 days to identify and contain (IBM and Ponemon Institute, 2026). ENISA observes that attackers abuse cyber dependencies, creating a “ripple effect across the supply chain” (ENISA, 2025).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ERead those numbers as direction, not precision. Each study defines “third party” and counts breaches differently. The direction is consistent: the more you rely on others, the more their weaknesses become yours.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"the-ordinary-mistakes\"\u003EThe ordinary mistakes\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EMost supply line failures are dull.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ENo list.\u003C\/strong\u003E You cannot defend dependencies you have not named.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ETrust by contract.\u003C\/strong\u003E A security questionnaire, filed once, and never looked at again.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EFlat access.\u003C\/strong\u003E A vendor account that can reach more than the vendor’s job needs.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EOne route.\u003C\/strong\u003E A single connectivity provider, a single cloud region, a single identity provider, a single payment rail.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ENo exit.\u003C\/strong\u003E No plan for the day a supplier is breached, suspended or simply gone.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ENIST’s CSF 2.0 turns this into a category of its own: Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management (GV.SC) under the Govern function. Its outcomes include that “suppliers are known and prioritized by criticality,” that requirements are “integrated into contracts and other types of agreements,” that supplier risks are “understood, recorded, prioritized, assessed, responded to, and monitored over the course of the relationship,” that relevant suppliers are “included in incident planning, response, and recovery activities,” and that plans cover what happens “after the conclusion of a partnership or service agreement” (NIST CSF 2.0, 2024).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThat list is the best brief I know. Map it onto your own contracts and see which lines are blank.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"triage-the-supply-line\"\u003ETriage the supply line\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EYou cannot treat every supplier alike. Sort them.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ctable\u003E\n\u003Cthead\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003ETier\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003EWho sits here\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003EWhat you do\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003C\/thead\u003E\n\u003Ctbody\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003E1. Cannot operate without\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EIdentity provider, core cloud platform, primary connectivity, payment processing, the one software package that runs the business\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EWritten security requirements; incident contact; right to be told; a tested fallback plan; an owner at senior level\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003E2. Painful to lose\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ECollaboration tools, CRM, HR systems, specialist SaaS\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EStandard security terms; access limited to what the job needs; a data export you have tested\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003E3. Replaceable\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EEverything else\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EBasic review; do not give broad access\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003C\/tbody\u003E\n\u003C\/table\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EFor tier 1, ask hard questions in writing. How would you tell us about an incident, and how fast? What do you do if your own supplier is breached? Where does our data live? How do we leave?\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"keep-the-rear-from-burning\"\u003EKeep the rear from burning\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECSIS offers a principle you can borrow from logistics: self-sufficiency (CSIS, 2025a). For networks, this means the ability to operate through a failure upstream, for a while.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EA second route for what matters.\u003C\/strong\u003E A second connectivity path. A second DNS provider. A backup identity path for administrators. Not for everything.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ELocal copies of what you need.\u003C\/strong\u003E Data exports of the systems that run the business, kept where you control them, in formats you can read without the vendor.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EManual procedures,\u003C\/strong\u003E printed and tested, for critical operations.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ELimits on blast radius.\u003C\/strong\u003E Treat vendor connections as untrusted. Give each its own segment, its own account and its own logging.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ENIST’s cyber resiliency guidance adds a warning that fits here. Redundancy-supporting approaches such as backup, surplus capacity and replication “are not sufficient to protect against” an advanced persistent threat. A threat actor might choose backup servers as “optimum locations to implant malware” if they are not sufficiently protected, and remote backup servers built with the same architecture as the primary may share its weakness (NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 2 Rev. 1, 2021). A second copy that shares the first copy’s weaknesses is the same line drawn twice. That is why diversity appears in the same list.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"software-dependencies\"\u003ESoftware dependencies\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ETreat software like any other supply: know what is in it. For critical applications, keep a software bill of materials, track which versions you run, and know who to ask when a component is announced as vulnerable. For the edge, the joint guidance lists “procure secure-by-design devices” among its seven strategies (NSA, 2025). You cannot always do that. When you cannot, the compensating control is to limit and monitor what the product can reach.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"exercise-the-break\"\u003EExercise the break\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ENIST’s guidance on incident response says incidents “occur frequently and cause far more damage,” and recovery “often takes weeks or months.” It also urges that lessons be shared as soon as they are identified, “not delayed until after recovery concludes” (NIST SP 800-61r3, 2025). For supply lines, that means exercising the day a tier 1 supplier fails or is breached. Who calls whom? What do we switch off? What do we tell customers? How long can we last?\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ERun it once a year. Invite the supplier if they will come.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"what-to-do_5\"\u003EWhat to do\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Col\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EBuild the supplier list.\u003C\/strong\u003E Name every tier 1 and tier 2 dependency. Record owner, data held, access given and exit path.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ETier them.\u003C\/strong\u003E Apply different rules to each tier.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EReview vendor access.\u003C\/strong\u003E Remove accounts and permissions that are not needed. Put multifactor authentication and logging on the rest.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EClose the dullest gaps first.\u003C\/strong\u003E A single route, no exit plan, no incident contact.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ETest one fallback.\u003C\/strong\u003E Pick the highest-impact tier 1 supplier and rehearse running without it.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EPut incident duties in contracts\u003C\/strong\u003E at renewal. Notification timelines, cooperation, data return.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EShare lessons early.\u003C\/strong\u003E Hold a short review after any supplier incident, before the dust settles.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ol\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"what-to-measure_4\"\u003EWhat to measure\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EShare of tier 1 suppliers with a named internal owner, a tested fallback and a documented incident contact.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ENumber of vendor accounts with access beyond their stated purpose.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ETime to run a critical process in fallback mode, in rehearsal.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EShare of tier 1 and tier 2 contracts that carry incident notification terms.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"part-vi-command\"\u003EPart VI: Command. Decide faster than the grind\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWhat public analysis describes.\u003C\/strong\u003E CSIS says the future is “shifting toward smaller, highly mobile, adaptable units, where field commanders are empowered to make decisions about cover, concealment, and tactics while minimizing their communications signature” (CSIS, 2025a). It says fast cycles of adaptation mean fronts may evolve at different paces, “necessitating central nodes to facilitate sharing lessons learned,” and that “units will need resilient mesh networks to ensure continuous communication even if multiple nodes go dark” (CSIS, 2025a). It reports a “six week learning cycle” attributed to a RUSI analyst, in which measures and countermeasures follow each other in weeks, not years (CSIS, 2025a). Another chapter says drone developers pushed innovation cycles to “weeks rather than months or years” (CSIS, 2025b).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThree ideas: decisions pushed to the edge, lessons pulled to the center, and communications that survive losing a node.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWhat it means for you.\u003C\/strong\u003E Command is the cross-cutting concern that decides whether all five fronts work together. It is not a rank. It is how decisions are made, how fast, by whom, and what happens when the person who normally decides is unreachable.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"the-decision-clock\"\u003EThe decision clock\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECompare two clocks.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EIBM’s 2026 study puts the mean time to identify and contain a breach at 247 days (IBM and Ponemon Institute, 2026). Verizon’s 2026 DBIR puts the median time to fully patch known-exploited vulnerabilities at 43 days, up from 32 (Verizon, 2026). Attack bursts, as shown in Part II, run in minutes and hours.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EAn organization whose decisions run on a slower clock than the pressure on it loses ground even when it is doing the right things. The target is not speed at any cost. The target is that no routine decision waits for a meeting.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"pre-decided-authority\"\u003EPre-decided authority\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EIn an incident you do not want to discover who can approve what. Decide it in advance.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EPre-authorized actions.\u003C\/strong\u003E A short list of actions that on-call staff may take without asking: disable an account, isolate a host, block an address range, revoke a token. Write down the conditions. Review them after use.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EEscalation triggers.\u003C\/strong\u003E Clear lines for when a decision moves up: a crown system, customer data, a regulator notice, a public statement, a payment.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EDelegation if unreachable.\u003C\/strong\u003E Every decision-maker has a named deputy with the same authority. The deputy has the numbers, the access, and the standing to act.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EIntent, not scripts.\u003C\/strong\u003E State what must be protected and what may be sacrificed. Let those closest to the problem choose the method.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThat last point is my own recommendation, drawn from the shape of the CSIS description. It is not a quotation from any doctrine. But the logic is the same as CSIS’s: distant, slow, centralized decisions fail under pressure, and local authority must be bounded by clear limits (CSIS, 2025a).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThe cost of delegation is mistakes. Accept some. Review them without punishing the people who acted in good faith. Otherwise nobody will act next time.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"lessons-to-the-center-fast\"\u003ELessons to the center, fast\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECSIS says a more widespread battlefield may see fronts evolve at different paces, “necessitating central nodes to facilitate sharing lessons learned” (CSIS, 2025a). NIST SP 800-61r3 says to share lessons “as soon as they are identified, not delayed until after recovery concludes” (NIST SP 800-61r3, 2025).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EFor you that means:\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EA running log\u003C\/strong\u003E kept during every incident and every near miss, with a short note on what worked and what did not.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EA weekly fifteen-minute review\u003C\/strong\u003E of the log. One owner. Output: at most three changes.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EA change channel\u003C\/strong\u003E where findings turn into tickets, with an owner and a date.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EOutside sources.\u003C\/strong\u003E Join an information-sharing community in your sector. Verizon’s own advice for the growing capability of attackers is to “maintain our footing and use collaboration and partnerships” (Verizon, 2026).\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EKeep the loop short. A lesson that waits for the quarterly meeting is a lesson that gets forgotten.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"communications-that-survive-a-lost-node\"\u003ECommunications that survive a lost node\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECSIS’s mesh-network idea has a plain analog: crisis communications that do not depend on the thing that failed (CSIS, 2025a). If email is down, how do you reach each other? If chat is down? If your identity provider is down and nobody can log in?\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EBuild a short communications plan:\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Col\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EA primary channel,\u003C\/strong\u003E the one you normally use.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EAn out-of-band channel\u003C\/strong\u003E that does not depend on your identity provider or primary network. Agree in advance which one, and who has the credentials.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EA phone tree\u003C\/strong\u003E on paper, kept current, with deputies.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EA rule\u003C\/strong\u003E for confirming that a message is real before acting on it, including voice and video, as in Part III.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ol\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ETest it quarterly. Ask the question: who did not get the message?\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"governance-without-ceremony\"\u003EGovernance without ceremony\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ENIST’s CSF 2.0 places Govern at the center of its six functions, alongside Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover (NIST CSF 2.0, 2024). That framing helps in practice. Governance is not paperwork. It is the set of decisions leadership has made, in advance, about what to protect, what to tolerate, and who decides.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EFor a mid-size organization, a one-page “risk appetite and decision rights” sheet may be the most useful governance document you can write. Name your crown assets. Name the maximum downtime you can accept for each. Name who may approve a deviation. Revisit it every six months.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"what-to-do_6\"\u003EWhat to do\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Col\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWrite the pre-authorized action list.\u003C\/strong\u003E Five to ten actions. Conditions. Owner. Review date.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EName deputies\u003C\/strong\u003E for every decision-maker, and give them access and authority.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EDraw the escalation triggers\u003C\/strong\u003E on one page.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EStart the lessons log\u003C\/strong\u003E and the weekly fifteen-minute review.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EBuild and test the out-of-band communications plan.\u003C\/strong\u003E\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWrite the one-page decision rights sheet\u003C\/strong\u003E and have leadership sign it.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ol\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"what-to-measure_5\"\u003EWhat to measure\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ETime from detection to first containment action, in incidents and exercises.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EShare of incident decisions made within pre-authorized limits.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ETime from a lesson identified to the change deployed.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EShare of the response team reached through the out-of-band channel within ten minutes, in a drill.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"part-vii-people\"\u003EPart VII: People. Endurance is the strategy\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWhat public analysis describes.\u003C\/strong\u003E CSIS notes that new drone units “require a vastly different skill set than traditional infantry” and that recruitment and training programs had to be intensified to build them (CSIS, 2025a). That sentence is generic. It says something every security leader knows: when the nature of the work changes, the people have to change with it, and it takes time.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECSIS also warns of leaning on technology as a crutch: “Using technology as a crutch happens today,” and that militaries “must be ready to lose those tools and keep fighting” (CSIS, 2025a). The same chapter says the human tendency to defer to machine recommendations is a hazard in itself (CSIS, 2025a).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWhat it means for you.\u003C\/strong\u003E People are the second cross-cutting concern, and in a war of attrition they are the scarcest resource. Tools can be bought. Experience cannot.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EISC2’s 2024 workforce study found 67% of respondents reported a staffing shortage and 90% reported one or more skills gaps (ISC2, 2024). Verizon’s analysis of small and medium-sized organizations found that most ransomware victims, among cases where size was known, were small or mid-size (Verizon, 2026). The ones with the smallest teams face the same cheap pressure as the ones with the largest.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EI do not cite burnout or turnover statistics here. The sources I opened for this paper do not measure them. I will say only what any security manager can see on their own team: sustained pressure, with no end date, wears people down.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"design-the-team-for-endurance\"\u003EDesign the team for endurance\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EA short fight can be won with heroics. A long grind cannot. The practical rules are not glamorous.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ERotate.\u003C\/strong\u003E Put on-call duty on a rota with real recovery time after a heavy shift. Do not let the same two people carry every incident.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ECross-train.\u003C\/strong\u003E For each critical function, name at least two people who can do it. Test it by having the second person do it, with the first person watching, once a quarter.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWrite it down.\u003C\/strong\u003E Runbooks for the ten things that go wrong most often, and the five that go wrong worst. Plain language. Tested by someone who did not write them.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EProtect attention.\u003C\/strong\u003E Cut alerts that never lead to action (see Part IV). Automate repetitive triage where you can, with human review (Part II). IBM found that extensive use of AI and automation in security was associated with a shorter breach lifecycle and lower costs (IBM and Ponemon Institute, 2026). Whatever you automate, keep a person accountable.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EKeep a bench.\u003C\/strong\u003E An incident response retainer, a managed detection provider, or a mutual-aid arrangement with a peer organization. Agree terms before you need them. Know who answers the phone at 3 a.m.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ETrain in the open.\u003C\/strong\u003E Exercises should include non-technical staff. Finance, legal, communications and executive assistants are part of the line. CSIS’s guidance on exercises is for militaries, but the principle carries over: simulate conditions where the adversary has good information (CSIS, 2025b). Assume they know your org chart.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"skills-that-matter-now\"\u003ESkills that matter now\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThe mix of skills changes as the fronts shift.
