A few that I would grow in a mid-size team:\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EIdentity and access.\u003C\/strong\u003E The craft of making access narrow and short-lived.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ECloud and third-party risk.\u003C\/strong\u003E Reading a provider’s responsibility model and finding where it leaves you exposed.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EDetection engineering.\u003C\/strong\u003E Turning a decision into a signal (Part IV).\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EResilience engineering.\u003C\/strong\u003E Backups, restores, failover and degraded operations (Parts III and V).\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ECommunication.\u003C\/strong\u003E Plain, calm writing and speaking under pressure. Underrated.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EYou will not hire all of them. Train, contract and partner.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"humans-and-machines\"\u003EHumans and machines\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECSIS’s cautionary note on AI is about judgment: when both sides use AI, the incentive is to defer to it, and for now that will lead to mistakes (CSIS, 2025a). Applied to security operations, it is a rule worth writing down:\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EAI recommends. A named human decides, for anything that affects customers, access or money.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EEach automated action has a log, an owner and an off switch.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EPeople review a sample of automated decisions every week and write down what they find.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ENobody is judged by how often they agree with the tool.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"morale-is-operational\"\u003EMorale is operational\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EI will keep this short. Say thank you. Name what went well in every post-incident review. Make sure people can take leave. Make sure the person who raised the alarm is thanked, not blamed. Those are cheap. They also decide whether your best people are still there in a year.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"what-to-do_7\"\u003EWhat to do\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Col\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EBuild the rota.\u003C\/strong\u003E Include recovery time. Name deputies.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EMap single points of human failure.\u003C\/strong\u003E For every critical function, name two people.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWrite and test ten runbooks.\u003C\/strong\u003E\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ESign a bench.\u003C\/strong\u003E Retainer, partner or mutual-aid agreement, with a tested contact path.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ERun a cross-functional exercise\u003C\/strong\u003E with finance, legal, communications and executives.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWrite the human-in-the-loop rule\u003C\/strong\u003E for AI and automation, and review a sample every week.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ol\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"what-to-measure_6\"\u003EWhat to measure\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ENumber of critical functions with fewer than two trained people.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EShare of runbooks tested by someone other than their author in the last six months.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EDistribution of on-call load across the team.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ETime to reach your outside bench in a test call.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"part-viii-scenarios\"\u003EPart VIII: Three scenarios\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThese three scenarios are \u003Cstrong\u003Ehypothetical\u003C\/strong\u003E. They are not reports of real incidents, real organizations or real results. They contain no statistics. They exist to show how the fronts interact, and to give your team something to rehearse.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EEach scenario is a mid-size organization, roughly a few hundred staff, with a small security team and several outside providers. Use them as prompts for a tabletop exercise. Replace the details with your own.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"scenario-one-the-long-week\"\u003EScenario one: The long week\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cem\u003EA regional services company. Monday to Friday.\u003C\/em\u003E\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EMonday.\u003C\/strong\u003E The edge. A vendor publishes a notice about a flaw in a remote access appliance. It is on the list of known-exploited vulnerabilities. The company runs that appliance. The patch window is scheduled for the following weekend because of a customer deadline.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ETuesday.\u003C\/strong\u003E Drones. A flood hits the customer portal for twenty minutes, stops, then returns an hour later. The on-call engineer spends the afternoon on the upstream mitigation. Meanwhile, a wave of phishing messages reaches finance and the help desk.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWednesday.\u003C\/strong\u003E Sensors. The scanning traffic against the appliance rises. The log source for the appliance has been quiet for days. Nobody noticed, because nobody was asked to watch it.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EThursday.\u003C\/strong\u003E Command. A help-desk call, convincingly polite, asks for a password reset for a senior manager who is traveling. The help-desk agent is under pressure and has no verification rule for resets.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWhat good looks like.\u003C\/strong\u003E\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EThe edge appliance is on the list of tier-1 internet-facing assets. The known-exploited flaw triggers a pre-authorized emergency patch outside the normal window. A named owner decides in hours, not days.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EThe flood runbook is rehearsed. The on-call engineer engages upstream protection by the book, and a second person checks the quiet systems while the loud one is being handled.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EA heartbeat check on the appliance’s logs fires on Tuesday, not after the fact.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EThe help-desk rule requires a call-back to a known number for any reset of a privileged or traveling executive’s account. The agent follows the rule, and nobody criticizes the delay.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EBy Friday the team has reviewed what happened, changed three things, and rested.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EQuestions for your tabletop.\u003C\/strong\u003E Who can approve an emergency patch outside the window? What do we turn off if the appliance cannot be patched in time? Who is watching the quiet log source?\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"scenario-two-the-quiet-clock\"\u003EScenario two: The quiet clock\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cem\u003EA professional services firm. A bad afternoon.\u003C\/em\u003E\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ESituation.\u003C\/strong\u003E A time source used by several internal systems begins to drift. The drift is small at first. Log timestamps no longer line up between systems. A certificate validation error appears on one internal service, then another. The help desk begins to receive reports of failed sign-ins.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EAt the same time, someone calls the finance team using a voice that sounds like the managing partner. It asks for an urgent payment to a new account, citing a confidential deal. The caller says not to discuss it by email.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EPressure points by front.\u003C\/strong\u003E\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EElectronic warfare, in the sense of Part III.\u003C\/strong\u003E Time and voice are both signals. Both can be wrong. The two events may be unrelated, or one may be covering for the other. The team does not know.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ESensors.\u003C\/strong\u003E Logs with inconsistent time make it hard to build a timeline. Analysts lose confidence in the data.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ECommand.\u003C\/strong\u003E Who decides whether to take an authentication service offline to investigate? Who decides whether the payment is real?\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EPeople.\u003C\/strong\u003E The finance clerk is junior. The caller is senior.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWhat good looks like.\u003C\/strong\u003E\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ETwo independent time sources are configured, and an alert fires when they disagree. The team switches to the second source under a runbook, rather than debating which clock is right.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EThe finance team has a rule: new payee, urgent request, any channel, requires out-of-band verification through a known number, and a second approver. The clerk follows it. The managing partner, called back on a number from the directory, knows nothing about it.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EIncident notes record the time source and the drift, so the timeline can be rebuilt later.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ELeadership has told the team, in advance, that following the rule is correct even when the person asking is the most senior in the firm.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EQuestions for your tabletop.\u003C\/strong\u003E Which of our systems would fail first if time were wrong? Who can stop a payment at 4:55 p.m. on a Friday? Have we tested this rule against someone who sounds exactly like the boss?\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"scenario-three-the-vendor-goes-dark\"\u003EScenario three: The vendor goes dark\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cem\u003EA distribution business. A supplier fails.\u003C\/em\u003E\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ESituation.\u003C\/strong\u003E A cloud service that handles the company’s orders is unavailable. The provider’s first notice is vague. Hours pass. Later, the provider states that it is investigating a security incident and that customer data may be affected. Staff cannot take orders. The managed service provider that administers part of the network is also affected, and its support line is overloaded.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EPressure points by front.\u003C\/strong\u003E\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ESupply lines.\u003C\/strong\u003E One provider carries a critical process. Customers are asking questions. The sales team wants to promise dates.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EPeople.\u003C\/strong\u003E Staff have been working through the night. The one person who understands the integration is on leave.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EWhat good looks like.\u003C\/strong\u003E\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EThe supplier is on the tier-1 list. The company holds a recent export of order data in a readable format, and a manual procedure for taking orders by phone and spreadsheet for a limited time. Staff have practiced it once.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EThe vendor connection runs through its own segment with its own account, restricted to what the integration needs. The company disables the connection on its own authority while the vendor investigates.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EA named incident owner decides what to tell customers and when. A short holding statement goes out early and is updated at set times.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EThe contract with the provider contains incident notification duties, which the company invokes. The rota gives the first person leave.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EQuestions for your tabletop.\u003C\/strong\u003E If this supplier were gone for a week, what would we do? Who may disable the connection? What would we say to customers in the first two hours?\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"what-the-scenarios-share\"\u003EWhat the scenarios share\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ENone of these events is exotic. Each is ordinary pressure applied from several directions. In every one, the organization that does well has done unglamorous work in advance: a list, a rule, a rehearsal, a named owner. The organization that does badly usually has the same tools. It has not decided what to do.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ERun one scenario a quarter. Change the details. Write down what you find.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch1 id=\"recommendations\"\u003ERecommendations\u003C\/h1\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EHere is the plan.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EIt is not glamorous. It is a campaign built around depth, cheap layers, second sources, a small signature, a rear that can burn, and decisions that do not wait for permission. The seven parts above each end with their own actions. This section puts them in order.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EAdd capability only when the controls and the evidence are in place. Timelines depend on your team size, your tooling and your risk appetite. The phases below are a sequence first and a schedule second.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"the-seven-moves\"\u003EThe seven Mark each strong, partial or absent.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EList your top signals (time, identity, names, voice, alerts) and note the second source for each, or the gap.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EWrite down today’s baseline: time to patch known-exploited flaws on the edge, share of exposed logins with MFA, time to restore a crown system, time from alert to first human action.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EBuild the supplier list and tier it.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EWrite the pre-authorized action list and name deputies.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Ch3 id=\"days-31-to-60-close-the-cheap-doors\"\u003EDays 31 to 60: Close the cheap doors\u003C\/h3\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EPatch the edge. Remove services nobody can justify. Put management interfaces behind a separate path.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ERequire MFA on every external login and remote access path, starting with administrators.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EConfirm upstream flood protection in writing. Run the two-hour drill.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EAdd heartbeat checks to critical log sources.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ESet verification rules for payments, credential resets and access requests. Brief the people who handle them.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EStand up the out-of-band communications path and test it once.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Ch3 id=\"days-61-to-90-rehearse-and-decide\"\u003EDays 61 to 90: Rehearse and decide\u003C\/h3\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ERun one scenario from Part VIII as a tabletop.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ERun a controlled test of removing the primary time source in a change window.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ETest the first fallback for your most important tier 1 supplier.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EStart the lessons log and the weekly review.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EWrite the one-page decision rights sheet and have leadership sign it.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ERe-measure the baseline. Report the change to leadership, including what did not move.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"the-first-12-months\"\u003EThe first 12 months\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Ctable\u003E\n\u003Cthead\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003EQuarter\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003EFocus\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003Cth\u003EWhat you deliver\u003C\/th\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003C\/thead\u003E\n\u003Ctbody\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EQ1 (days 1 to 90)\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EMap, close, rehearse\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EEverything in the 90-day plan\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EQ2\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EDig deeper\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ESegment your most valuable systems; separate administrator access; extend phishing-resistant authentication to all staff who touch crown assets\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EQ3\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ESee and decide\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EDecision-led detection for the six key decisions; first decoys; automation in recommend-only mode, then limited authority; second tabletop with finance, legal and communications\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003Ctr\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EQ4\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003ESurvive and adapt\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EA full tier 1 supplier failure exercise; contract terms updated at renewal; re-run the self-assessment; set next year’s targets from your own results\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003C\/tbody\u003E\n\u003C\/table\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThroughout the year:\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EEvery widening of authority is a decision,\u003C\/strong\u003E made by a named owner, documented and reversible.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EEvery incident and near miss feeds the lessons log.\u003C\/strong\u003E\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EEvery quarter, report to leadership\u003C\/strong\u003E on the metrics and on what went wrong.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EEvery year, re-run the self-assessment\u003C\/strong\u003E below.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"self-assessment-checklist\"\u003ESelf-assessment checklist\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EUse this checklist with your security, IT and leadership teams. Answer honestly. A “no” is not a failure. It is a work item.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EScore each item: 0 = not in place, 1 = partly in place, 2 = fully in place and evidenced. The levels at the end are my rough guide, not a formal standard.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch3 id=\"trenches\"\u003ETrenches\u003C\/h3\u003E\n\u003Cul class=\"checklist\"\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; The trench map exists and is reviewed at least twice a year.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; Administrators use a separate access path with phishing-resistant authentication.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; Crown systems sit in segments that an ordinary workstation cannot reach, and this has been tested.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; A restore of a crown system from isolated backup has been rehearsed in the last year.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Ch3 id=\"drones\"\u003EDrones\u003C\/h3\u003E\n\u003Cul class=\"checklist\"\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; MFA protects every externally exposed login and every remote access path.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; Known-exploited vulnerabilities on internet-facing systems have a target patch time, and it is measured.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; Upstream flood protection is in place, with a written runbook and a rehearsal.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; Automated actions run under a human-in-the-loop rule, with logs and an off switch.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Ch3 id=\"electronic-warfare\"\u003EElectronic warfare\u003C\/h3\u003E\n\u003Cul class=\"checklist\"\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; Critical systems use at least two independent time sources, and disagreement raises an alert.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; Requests to move money, reset credentials or grant access follow an out-of-band verification rule.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; A critical process has been run in degraded mode in the last year.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; An out-of-band management path exists for the most critical systems.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Ch3 id=\"sensors\"\u003ESensors\u003C\/h3\u003E\n\u003Cul class=\"checklist\"\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; An outside-in list of internet-facing assets exists and has been reconciled with the asset register.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; Every alert has an owner and a response time.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; Every critical log source has a heartbeat check.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; Public repositories, shared links and storage have been reviewed for exposed secrets and files in the last six months.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Ch3 id=\"supply-lines\"\u003ESupply lines\u003C\/h3\u003E\n\u003Cul class=\"checklist\"\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; A supplier list exists, with tiers, owners, data held and access granted.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; Vendor accounts are limited to what each integration needs, with MFA and logging.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; Data exports for tier 1 and tier 2 systems are kept where you control them, in formats you can read.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; A tier 1 supplier failure has been exercised in the last year.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; Tier 1 contracts contain incident notification and cooperation terms.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Ch3 id=\"command\"\u003ECommand\u003C\/h3\u003E\n\u003Cul class=\"checklist\"\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; A pre-authorized action list exists, with conditions and review dates.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; Every decision-maker has a named deputy with access and authority.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; A lessons log is kept, with a weekly review and an owner.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; An out-of-band communications path exists, and it has been tested in the last quarter.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Ch3 id=\"people\"\u003EPeople\u003C\/h3\u003E\n\u003Cul class=\"checklist\"\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; The on-call rota includes recovery time, and load is shared.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; Every critical function has at least two trained people.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; Runbooks exist for the ten most likely and five worst failures, and someone other than the author has tested them.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; An outside bench (retainer, partner or mutual aid) exists, with a tested contact path.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E☐\u0026nbsp; Exercises include finance, legal, communications and executives.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Ch3 id=\"reading-your-score\"\u003EReading your score\u003C\/h3\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThere are 30 items, for a maximum of 60 points.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003E0–19: Foundational.\u003C\/strong\u003E Map the ground, close the cheap doors, and fix single points of failure before anything else.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003E20–39: Developing.\u003C\/strong\u003E The basics are partly in place. Prioritize second sources, supplier fallbacks and decision rights.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003E40–60: Established.\u003C\/strong\u003E Deepen segmentation, automate with care, and keep rehearsing.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EWhatever your score, the next step is the same: pick the three lowest items that matter most to your risk, assign owners and dates, and re-score in a quarter.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2 id=\"a-starter-scorecard\"\u003EA starter scorecard\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EReport these to leadership each quarter. people\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EPeople\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003Ctd\u003EDown\u003C\/td\u003E\n\u003C\/tr\u003E\n\u003C\/tbody\u003E\n\u003C\/table\u003E\n\u003Ch1 id=\"conclusion\"\u003EConclusion\u003C\/h1\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThe sources agree on direction.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EExploitation of known flaws is still a leading way in. Credentials still get stolen and used. Floods and bots arrive every day. Suppliers carry more of your risk each year. Breaches that run long cost more. Teams are short of people and skills (Verizon, 2026; IBM and Ponemon Institute, 2026; ISC2, 2024).\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThe public analysis of the modern battlefield points the same way. Depth. Cheap mass. Spoofed and jammed signals. Constant observation. Supply lines that are never safe. Fast cycles of measure and countermeasure (CSIS, 2025a; CSIS, 2025b; CSIS, 2025c). Your organization is not at a front line. But it works in the same electromagnetic and informational weather, and it faces the same economics: cheap pressure against costly defense.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EYou will not win that by matching them effort for effort. You win it the way resilient institutions do.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EDig in, so the first breach is not the last line. Spread out, so one failure does not take everything. Keep a second source, so a false signal does not steer you. Know what the outside can see, and make sense of what your own sensors tell you. Keep the rear from burning, and know how to fight when it does. Push decisions to the people closest to the problem, and learn faster than the grind wears you down.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EAbove all, keep going. This is a long contest, and the organizations that do well in it are the ones that are still doing the boring work in year three.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EInfinitum Corporation helps organizations take these steps in a way that fits their size, systems and risk appetite. I make no promise about the outcome any organization will achieve, and every figure in this paper belongs to the source cited.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EDon’t take my word for it. Read the sources, then decide.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThis is the second paper in a series. The first is \u003Cem\u003EDead Reckoning: AI for Security Operations in a Jammed, Spoofed, Watched World\u003C\/em\u003E. The next is \u003Cem\u003EBreak It Before They Do: Authorized Hacking for Organizations Under Siege\u003C\/em\u003E.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ELet’s stay engaged. Sources were opened and read between October 25 and 26, 2026. Where a source is quoted, the words are the source’s own. Where a number is cited, it belongs to that source and describes that source’s dataset.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cem\u003ENote on neutrality.\u003C\/em\u003E This paper draws general lessons about technology and conflict from public sources. It takes no side and makes no claim about any party. Where a source attributes events or reports figures about specific parties, those attributions and figures are left out here. Titles of the CSIS report and chapters are shortened to keep this paper party-neutral. The URLs lead to the full originals.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch1 id=\"glossary\"\u003EGlossary\u003C\/h1\u003E\n\u003Cdiv class=\"glossary\"\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EATT\u0026amp;CK.\u003C\/strong\u003E MITRE’s knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world observations, used to map detections and find coverage gaps.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EAttrition.\u003C\/strong\u003E A contest won by endurance and cost exchange, not by a single decisive event.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EBlast radius.\u003C\/strong\u003E How far the damage from one compromised account, device or supplier can spread.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ECSF 2.0.\u003C\/strong\u003E The NIST Cybersecurity Framework version 2.0, organized around six functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ECrown assets.\u003C\/strong\u003E The systems and data whose loss would most damage the organization.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EDDoS (distributed denial of service).\u003C\/strong\u003E An attack that floods a service with traffic from many sources so that legitimate users cannot reach it.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EDeception (defensive).\u003C\/strong\u003E Placing decoy assets, credentials or data inside your own environment so that intruders who interact with them reveal themselves. Always with legal sign-off.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EEdge device.\u003C\/strong\u003E A firewall, router, VPN gateway or other system that sits between your internal network and the internet.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EElectronic warfare (EW).\u003C\/strong\u003E The use of the electromagnetic spectrum to jam, spoof or otherwise disrupt signals, and the defense against that.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EGNSS.\u003C\/strong\u003E Global navigation satellite systems, such as GPS, which provide location and timing.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EImplicit trust zone.\u003C\/strong\u003E An area in which every entity is trusted because of where it sits, not because of what it has proved. NIST says it should be as small as possible.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EIrregular warfare.\u003C\/strong\u003E Joint doctrine describes it as “indirect, non-attributable, or asymmetric” competition. Used in this paper as an analytic lens only.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EISR.\u003C\/strong\u003E Intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EJamming.\u003C\/strong\u003E Deliberate interference that blocks a radio signal.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EKEV.\u003C\/strong\u003E CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog: flaws with evidence of active exploitation.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EMFA (multifactor authentication).\u003C\/strong\u003E Requiring more than a password to sign in. Phishing-resistant forms resist being relayed to an attacker.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EOut-of-band.\u003C\/strong\u003E Using a separate channel, such as a known phone number, to verify a request or to manage a system, so that one failure does not take out both.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EPNT.\u003C\/strong\u003E Positioning, navigation and timing.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ESegmentation.\u003C\/strong\u003E Dividing a network into zones so that a compromise in one does not spread freely to others.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ESpoofing.\u003C\/strong\u003E Deliberately sending false signals or data so that a system displays or accepts something incorrect.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003ETabletop exercise.\u003C\/strong\u003E A discussion-based rehearsal in which a team walks through a scenario and decides what it would do.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cstrong\u003EZero trust.\u003C\/strong\u003E In NIST’s words, an evolving set of cybersecurity paradigms that move defenses from static, network-based perimeters to a focus on users, assets and resources.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003C\/div\u003E\u003C\/main\u003E\n\u003Cscript type=\"application\/ld+json\"\u003E\n{\n \"@context\": \"https:\/\/schema.org\",\n Customers, employees, investors, regulators and the public each decide what a company is worth based on how they understand it, and that understanding is shaped every day by competitors, journalists, algorithms and, increasingly, hostile actors. \u003Cstrong\u003ECorporate Cognitive Warfare\u003C\/strong\u003E, a term coined by William Aaron Turner, Founder and President of Infinitum Corporation, is the discipline of competing on that terrain lawfully and defending it well.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThe expanded edition grows the original paper to about 15,000 words. It keeps the original structure, definitions and six-phase framework (Understand, Shape, Seed, Amplify, Exploit, Protect) and adds four bodies of material:\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cscript Cognitive Warfare: A Doctrine Introduction"},"content":{"type":"html","$t":"\u003Cdiv style=\"background: rgb(255, 255, 255); color: #111111; font-family: Georgia, \u0026quot;Times New Roman\u0026quot;, serif; font-size: 17px; line-height: 1.7; margin: 0px auto; max-width: 720px;\"\u003E\n\u003Cdiv class=\"separator\" style=\"clear: both; text-align: center;\"\u003E\u003Ca href=\"https:\/\/blogger.googleusercontent.com\/img\/b\/R29vZ2xl\/AVvXsEiRSUFq40U3vPtactJlFgH4m-hTB5HGwuDYWC8CQEw4uwkkugGNfQ2naAUg3dy63QkRhAN0lHY054DkqRwiIjba5qKWicG-1t6kZe-_BA2i18rJeCE4pM_CD3rbR51DUPm9ECbLptq6-bXZCQXimtmNC-jIVcJgTYmzkeh3oTJ7W0cB1LZnnUkp7ZOdgXun\/s1600\/wp-cover-ccw.jpg\" style=\"margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;\"\u003E\u003Cimg alt=\"Corporate Cognitive Warfare: A Doctrine Introduction\" border=\"0\" data-original-height=\"900\" data-original-width=\"1600\" height=\"900\" src=\"https:\/\/blogger.googleusercontent.com\/img\/b\/R29vZ2xl\/AVvXsEiRSUFq40U3vPtactJlFgH4m-hTB5HGwuDYWC8CQEw4uwkkugGNfQ2naAUg3dy63QkRhAN0lHY054DkqRwiIjba5qKWicG-1t6kZe-_BA2i18rJeCE4pM_CD3rbR51DUPm9ECbLptq6-bXZCQXimtmNC-jIVcJgTYmzkeh3oTJ7W0cB1LZnnUkp7ZOdgXun\/s1600\/wp-cover-ccw.jpg\" style=\"height: auto; max-width: 100%;\" width=\"1600\" \/\u003E\u003C\/a\u003E\u003C\/div\u003E\n\u003Cp style=\"border-left: 4px solid rgb(176, 0, 0); color: #333333; font-style: italic; padding-left: 12px;\"\u003EBy William Aaron Turner, CEO of \u003Ca href=\"https:\/\/www.theinfinitumcorporation.com\" rel=\"noopener\" style=\"color: #b00000;\"\u003EInfinitum Corporation\u003C\/a\u003E, who coined the term \"Corporate Cognitive Warfare\"\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003E\u003Cb\u003EYour next competitor may never touch your price.\u003C\/b\u003E It may simply decide what your market notices, remembers and believes about you, before a buyer ever opens a spreadsheet. That contest is already under way, and most companies are fighting it without a doctrine.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EI call that doctrine \u003Cb\u003ECorporate Cognitive Warfare\u003C\/b\u003E (CCW). I coined the term to describe something I kept seeing in my work at Infinitum Corporation: the ideas that states and militaries use to think about perception, attention and decision-making have direct, lawful lessons for how companies compete and how they defend themselves. This post is the introduction. The expanded white paper follows.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\n\u003Ch2 style=\"border-bottom: 3px solid rgb(176, 0, 0); color: black; padding-bottom: 4px;\"\u003EWhat Corporate Cognitive Warfare is\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECorporate Cognitive Warfare is the disciplined application of irregular-warfare thinking to the corporate competitive environment. It treats the minds of customers, employees, investors, partners and regulators as the ground where competition is actually decided. Conventional marketing asks, \"How do we promote this product?\" CCW asks a harder question: \"How does our market perceive reality, where does its attention go, and how are its decisions made, and how do we earn our place in that process honestly?\"\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EIt is not a new word for advertising. It is a way of organizing everything a company says and does around one objective: winning the contest for perception, attention and decision-making, and protecting the company when someone else tries to win that contest at its expense.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\n\u003Ch2 style=\"border-bottom: 3px solid rgb(176, 0, 0); color: black; padding-bottom: 4px;\"\u003EThe four core messages\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Col\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cb\u003EMarkets are now cognitive battlespaces.\u003C\/b\u003E Attention and perception decide outcomes before price does. By the time a buyer compares offers, the shortlist has usually already been shaped by what they saw, searched for and heard from people they trust.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cb\u003EMilitary doctrine holds lessons, studied neutrally.\u003C\/b\u003E CCW adapts concepts from published military literature to lawful corporate strategy. That includes Russian reflexive control, Chinese cognitive domain operations and Western information operations. We study these traditions analytically. We take no side, make no claim about any state or party, and borrow lessons about how perception and decisions work, never methods of deception.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cb\u003EFive disciplines do the work.\u003C\/b\u003E Guerrilla marketing, marketing psychological operations (ethical persuasion), algorithmic discovery, social influence and precision paid media, described below.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cb\u003EDefense matters too.\u003C\/b\u003E Companies are targets. CCW helps them detect and counter disinformation, narrative attacks and competitor manipulation aimed at them.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ol\u003E\n\n\u003Ch2 style=\"border-bottom: 3px solid rgb(176, 0, 0); color: black; padding-bottom: 4px;\"\u003EWhat the doctrine borrows, and what it doesn't\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EReflexive control, as described in the analytic literature, is the idea of shaping the information an opponent uses so that they reach a decision on their own. Writing on cognitive domain operations treats human cognition itself as a domain to be contested. Western information operations doctrine frames the information environment as a place where outcomes are won or lost.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThe corporate lesson from all three is the same, and it's a defensive one as much as an offensive one: \u003Cb\u003Edecisions are shaped upstream, by what people see first, what they hear from people they trust, and how a problem is framed for them.\u003C\/b\u003E A company that understands this can present its truth more clearly. A company that ignores it leaves the framing to someone else.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EWhat CCW does not borrow is deception. The doctrine is about understanding the contest, not copying the tactics that make some state campaigns notorious.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\n\u003Ch2 style=\"border-bottom: 3px solid rgb(176, 0, 0); color: black; padding-bottom: 4px;\"\u003EThe five disciplines\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cb\u003EGuerrilla marketing.\u003C\/b\u003E Fast, low-cost activations that reframe the conversation in your favor and use timing windows larger competitors are too slow to reach.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cb\u003EMarketing psychological operations (ethical persuasion).\u003C\/b\u003E Evidence-based messaging and positioning that respect how people actually decide, through identity, social proof and clear framing, without misleading anyone.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cb\u003EAlgorithmic discovery.\u003C\/b\u003E Legitimate SEO, GEO (generative-engine optimization), keyword and hashtag architecture and smart timing, so you are the answer people and AI systems find first.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cb\u003ESocial influence.\u003C\/b\u003E Authentic advocacy from real employees, clients and creators, who share in their own words because they choose to.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cb\u003EPrecision paid media.\u003C\/b\u003E Sequenced, clearly labeled campaigns that reinforce organic work and reach the decision-makers who matter.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\n\u003Ch2 style=\"border-bottom: 3px solid rgb(176, 0, 0); color: black; padding-bottom: 4px;\"\u003EThe defensive side: narrative defense\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EEvery company with something worth taking has a narrative worth attacking. Disinformation about a product, a coordinated pile-on, a manipulated review profile or a rumor timed to a funding round can all damage trust faster than a press office can respond.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ECCW treats defense as a core discipline, not an afterthought. In practice that means:\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cb\u003ESensing:\u003C\/b\u003E monitoring how your company is described across search, social platforms and AI answers, so changes are seen early.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cb\u003ERecognition:\u003C\/b\u003E knowing what fake accounts, bot amplification, astroturfing and fabricated reviews look like, so they are identified as threats rather than mistaken for genuine sentiment.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cb\u003EResponse:\u003C\/b\u003E answering with verifiable facts, credible voices and the reporting tools platforms provide, quickly and calmly.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Cb\u003EResilience:\u003C\/b\u003E building enough earned trust beforehand that a narrative attack meets an audience that already knows who you are.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\n\u003Ch2 style=\"border-bottom: 3px solid rgb(176, 0, 0); color: black; padding-bottom: 4px;\"\u003ELawful and ethical boundaries\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EA doctrine with the word \"warfare\" in it needs firm limits, so here they are. Corporate Cognitive Warfare as Infinitum Corporation practices it is lawful and platform-compliant only.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cul style=\"border-left: 4px solid rgb(176, 0, 0); padding-left: 28px;\"\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ENo fabrication, disinformation or false claims.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ENo fake accounts, sock puppets or bot amplification.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ENo fake or purchased reviews.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ENo paid endorsements without clear disclosure.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ENo coordinated inauthentic behavior.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ERespect for advertising, competition and privacy law, and for each platform's rules.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EThose deceptive tactics appear in CCW only as threats to recognize and defend against. Trust is the center of gravity. Any gain that spends trust to buy attention is a loss.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\n\u003Ch2 style=\"border-bottom: 3px solid rgb(176, 0, 0); color: black; padding-bottom: 4px;\"\u003EWhy this matters now\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003ESearch is turning into answers. Feeds decide what people see. Buyers trust peers more than brochures. In that environment a company doesn't just need a good product and a fair price. It needs a deliberate strategy for how it is perceived, and a plan for when someone tries to rewrite that perception. Corporate Cognitive Warfare is that strategy, and the plan that goes with it.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\n\u003Ch2 style=\"border-bottom: 3px solid rgb(176, 0, 0); color: black; padding-bottom: 4px;\"\u003EFurther reading\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Ca href=\"https:\/\/doi.org\/10.1080\/13518040490450529\" rel=\"noopener\" style=\"color: #b00000;\"\u003ERussia's Reflexive Control Theory and the Military\u003C\/a\u003E (Journal of Slavic Military Studies)\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003E\u003Ca href=\"https:\/\/www.airuniversity.af.edu\/CASI\/Display\/Article\/3273289\/how-china-wins-the-cognitive-domain\/\" rel=\"noopener\" style=\"color: #b00000;\"\u003EHow China Wins the Cognitive Domain\u003C\/a\u003E (China Aerospace Studies Institute, Air University)\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\n\u003Cdiv style=\"background: rgb(0, 0, 0); border-top: 5px solid rgb(176, 0, 0); color: white; margin: 28px 0px; padding: 18px 20px;\"\u003E\n\u003Ch2 style=\"color: white; margin-top: 0px;\"\u003ERead the full white paper\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Ca href=\"https:\/\/infinitumwhitepapers.blogspot.com\/2026\/10\/corporate-cognitive-warfare-expanded.html\" style=\"color:#ffffff;font-weight:bold;\"\u003ECorporate Cognitive Warfare: The Expanded Edition\u003C\/a\u003E \u0026middot; \u003Ca href=\"https:\/\/doi.org\/10.5281\/zenodo.23838097\" style=\"color:#ffffff;\"\u003EDOI 10.5281\/zenodo.23838097\u003C\/a\u003E\n  \u003Cp style=\"margin-bottom: 0px;\"\u003EThe expanded white paper, \u003Ci\u003ECorporate Cognitive Warfare: Irregular Warfare for Market Supremacy\u003C\/i\u003E, is forthcoming. It covers the doctrinal foundations, each discipline in depth, an operational framework, illustrative use cases and a full section on defense and counter-influence. The link will appear here when it is published.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003C\/div\u003E\n\n\u003Cp style=\"color: #333333; font-style: italic;\"\u003E\"Corporate Cognitive Warfare\" is a term coined by Figures are attributed to the sources cited.\u003C\/b\u003E\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EOh, the pearl-clutching from Western capitals.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EIn April 2022 the IMF projected that Russia's economy would shrink 8.5% in 2022. The IMF's current numbers show -1.4% in 2022, then +4.1% in 2023 and +4.9% in 2024. When a forecast misses by that much, the sensible question is what the model missed.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EMy new Infinitum Corporation paper, \u003Cb\u003E\"Russia's State-Influenced Capitalism: Sanctions-Proof, War-Proof, and Chaos-Proof,\"\u003C\/b\u003E makes the argument. It is an argued position, with every figure attributed to its source.\u003C\/p\u003E\n\u003Ch2\u003EWhat it covers\u003C\/h2\u003E\n\u003Cul\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EThe 1990s, by the numbers: real GDP down 44%, prices up 874% in 1993, life expectancy down almost five years (World Bank).\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ESanctions: more than twice as many designations as Iran, Syria and North Korea combined (Castellum.AI), and no collapse.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EThe balance sheet: public debt of 16.6% of GDP, unemployment of 2.2% (IMF, 2025).\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003ESafety, honestly: homicide down about 76% since 1994, but still above the United States. The paper says so.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003Cli\u003EA full chapter on what the critics get right: inflation, a 14% key rate, 1.0% growth, a heavy military burden, demographics and corruption perception.\u003C\/li\u003E\n\u003C\/ul\u003E\n\u003Cp\u003EPro-Russian, results-focused, and sourced to the last decimal. My advice for security operations is the same. Govern first. Measure a baseline. Pilot with analysts in the loop. Keep an independent check on every critical signal.
